articles.title: In 2005, Seattle began restoring neglected urban forests with volunteers; two decades later, 1.5 million native plants have been planted, and more than 2,000 acres are under restoration, earning a UN honour
articles.summary: A forest does not need to be replanted from scratch to be brought back to life.
articles.body: A forest does not need to be replanted from scratch to be brought back to life. Sometimes, all it takes is a little collective effort and a community willing to restore what has been neglected. We saw during COVID-19 how reduced human activity made some environmental changes more visible: birds returned, animals were spotted in cities, fish swam in rivers where people had once hesitated to dip their feet, and mountains became visible from miles away.In Seattle, thousands of volunteers have spent the past two decades doing exactly that: not starting something new, but saving what is already there. What began in 2005 as an effort to revive neglected urban forests has grown into a major restoration initiative, with more than 1.5 million native plants planted and over 2,000 acres brought under restoration. The work has now earned the city a United Nations honour.According to the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the Green Seattle Partnership has been recognised as a World Restoration Flagship under the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, following two decades of community-led efforts to revive the city's neglected urban forests.Seattle Mayor Katie B. Wilson said in a statement published by the UN Decade, “Through partnership, community stewardship of Seattle’s forested parklands has blossomed.” She also said, “We are honored to share the successful effort and our continued learning with cities around the world as part of the World Restoration Flagship programme.”How a community came together to restore Seattle's urban forestsThe Green Seattle Partnership was launched in 2005 as a collaboration between the City of Seattle and the community to address the deteriorating condition of its urban forests. Over the years, many of the city's forested parklands had been affected by invasive plant species, declining native vegetation and a lack of regular maintenance. These changes threatened the natural habitats of local wildlife and the ecological health of the forests.Rather than treating forest restoration as the sole responsibility of government agencies, the initiative brought together residents, volunteers, environmental organisations and city departments. People began coming forward voluntarily and dedicating their time to the cause. And this shows something very profound: everything is not the government's responsibility. The city is ours too, and looking after it is our duty just as much as it is the government's.The partnership also focused on ensuring that restoration was not a one-time activity. Volunteers continued returning to the same sites to maintain the newly planted vegetation and prevent invasive species from taking over again. This long-term approach helped transform the initiative from a city-led environmental programme into a community-driven effort.“I set out alone toward my destination, yet people kept joining in, and a caravan was formed.” Legendary Urdu poet Majrooh Sultanpuri wrote these words, and that is what happened in Seattle. Over the years, thousands of residents came forward and contributed their time and effort to the programme, demonstrating how collective participation can help protect and restore natural spaces within a growing city.From neglected parklands to a restoration success storyWhat makes it remarkable is not just the number of plants it has introduced, but the scale of the restoration work carried out over the years. According to the partnership's 20-year report, more than 2,032 acres of land across over 230 parks were under active restoration as of September 2025. The initiative had also recorded more than 1.5 million native plants planted, including over 355,000 trees.The contribution of volunteers has been equally significant. Since its launch in 2005, the partnership has received more than 1.4 million hours of volunteer work, with young people accounting for approximately 23 per cent of the total. It has also trained nearly 500 volunteer Forest Stewards, who organise restoration activities and encourage residents to take responsibility for the natural spaces in their neighbourhoods.Seattle's Green Seattle Partnership shows how the restoration of nature does not always require grand projects or large-scale interventions. Sometimes, all it takes is a small initiative and a sense of togetherness to make a big difference. It all begins with people coming together to protect what already exists and ensure that it continues to thrive. What started as an effort to revive neglected urban forests has, over two decades, grown into a movement involving thousands of residents and millions of native plants. Its recognition by the United Nations is not just an honour for Seattle, but also an example of how community participation can play a vital role in restoring urban ecosystems. As cities continue to expand, the initiative offers an important reminder that development and nature need not always come at the expense of one another.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Texas couple sold their home with $259,490 in net proceeds, but a $150,000 second mortgage complicated the divorce payout; appeals judges cut the wife's additional monetary award from $92,426 to $18,369
articles.summary: A Texas appeals court has reduced a monetary award granted to a woman following her divorce, ruling that a lower court's calculation gave her more than
articles.body: A Texas appeals court has reduced a monetary award granted to a woman following her divorce, ruling that a lower court's calculation gave her more than she was entitled to under the original settlement.The Fourteenth Court of Appeals in Houston modified the judgment involving Charles Kimathi Murungi and Sarah Kawinzi on November 17, 2026, reducing the additional amount payable to Kawinzi from $92,426.44 to $18,369.25. The court, however, upheld the rest of the lower court's judgment as modified.The dispute centred on the sale of the couple's former marital home and a $150,000 second mortgage that Murungi had been ordered to repay himself.How the $150,000 mortgage led to the disputeMurungi filed for divorce in October 2022. In 2023, he took out a $150,000 second mortgage, also referred to as the Discover Loan, to fund an agreed buyout of Kawinzi's share in the home's equity.Their divorce was finalised on May 31, 2024. Under the decree, the former marital residence was to be sold through a receiver, with the net proceeds divided equally between the two.The decree also specified that the second mortgage was Murungi's separate liability and that he was solely responsible for repaying it. If he failed to clear the loan before the house was sold, the receiver could adjust the distribution to ensure that the outstanding amount was borne entirely by him.However, the appeals court noted that Murungi had kept the entire loan amount in his personal bank account and used it for his own benefit instead of buying out Kawinzi's equity interest as agreed.When the house was sold in 2025, the net proceeds stood at $259,490.31. Since Murungi had not repaid the second mortgage, $148,114.40 was deducted from the sale proceeds to clear the outstanding loan and the property's title.This left $111,375.91 in the receiver's account.Why the appeals court reduced the awardIn November 2025, the trial court awarded Kawinzi the entire remaining $111,375.91, along with an additional monetary judgment of $92,426.44 against Murungi.Murungi challenged the calculation, arguing that it effectively made him liable twice for the same financial obligation.The appeals court agreed that the lower court had calculated the disbursement incorrectly.It said the original divorce decree entitled each party to half of the $259,490.31 net proceeds, or $129,745.16 each. Had Murungi repaid the second mortgage using his separate funds as ordered, Kawinzi would have received that amount.The appeals court ruled that awarding her $203,802.35 in total amounted to a windfall and violated the original 50-50 property division.It therefore reduced the additional monetary judgment to $18,369.25, bringing Kawinzi's total award to $129,745.16.The court dismissed five of Murungi's seven appeal claims, including challenges to the original property division, travel restrictions and child support calculations, saying it lacked jurisdiction to revisit the final divorce decree because he had not appealed it within the prescribed period.The modified judgment was affirmed.You use AI every day. articles.title: Peterhead museum secures £4m lottery funding
articles.summary: The Arbuthnot House complex will celebrate the heritage of the town and wider Aberdeenshire region.
articles.body:
Lottery funding of £4m has been announced for a new museum project taking shape in Aberdeenshire.

Construction began on the development of Peterhead's Arbuthnot House complex in June this year.

The museum dedicated to the region's history is expected to open in late 2028.

It will also house the town's library, a shop and cafe.

More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

The money from the National Lottery Heritage Fund will go towards fitting out the building, including audio-visual installations, specialist lighting, and display cases for exhibits.

Aberdeenshire Council said the museum would offer visitors new ways to discover and celebrate the stories, people and places that have shaped the area.

Originally a private home dating back to 1768, the B-listed Arbuthnot House served as a council building for many years before falling out of use.

The attraction will be Aberdeenshire's first shire-wide museum, showcasing some of the local authority's extensive heritage collections and artwork, with many items to be seen by the public for the first time.

It will feature permanent galleries and temporary exhibition spaces, as well as learning and workshop facilities, a restaurant with outdoor terrace, and community-focused exhibition areas.

The museum is part of Aberdeenshire's wider Cultural Tides project.

It is being supported through capital funding from the council, a UK government grant, and financial contributions from other bodies including Historic Environment Scotland.

Caroline Clark, The National Lottery Heritage Fund's director for Scotland, said it would be "a remarkable new cultural destination" celebrating and sharing the rich heritage of Peterhead and the wider region.

She added: "This project will open up important collections to new audiences, create opportunities for people to engage with their local heritage and ensure that treasured stories, objects and places are protected and enjoyed for generations to come."

Once completed the museum will also house Peterhead Library, and form the centrepiece of a new cultural quarter planned for the town.

Earlier proposals to re-use the town's previous library building as an events space were shelved due to rising costs.

Aberdeenshire Council co-leader Anne Stirling welcomed the new funding.

She said: "This will be a museum for Aberdeenshire, showcasing the inspiring individuals, rich heritage and amazing culture and artefacts which make the north-east unique."

articles.title: Pennsylvania woman arrested after taking back her repossessed car, which police had listed as stolen; man driving it with her permission spent two weeks in jail
articles.summary: A Pennsylvania woman was arrested after taking her own car from a storage lot where a loan company had repossessed it.
articles.body: A Pennsylvania woman was arrested after taking her own car from a storage lot where a loan company had repossessed it. The company had seized the vehicle after she defaulted on a loan secured against it. However, the woman remained its registered owner, with the lender listed only as a lienholder.After she drove the car away, the storage lot owner reported it stolen, and a Pennsylvania State Police trooper entered it as stolen in a national crime database. Two weeks later, police arrested Timothy Edwards while he was driving the car with the woman's permission. In a memorandum opinion issued on 21 May 2025, the US District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania examined the case. The woman, Ayana Alburg, was later arrested and charged with theft offences. Both subsequently filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the officers and local authorities involved.How did Alburg driving her repossessed BMW away lead to a stolen-car reportAyana Alburg had obtained a loan from Auto Equity Loans of DE, LLC, using her 2006 BMW X5 as security. The loan carried an annual percentage rate of 300%, which the court noted was illegal under Pennsylvania civil and criminal law. After Alburg defaulted, the company hired Top Notch Recovery, Inc. to repossess the vehicle for AEL.On 3 August 2018, Alburg went to Top Notch’s lot to collect her personal possessions. While the lot attendant and owner, Christopher Smith, was with another person, she drove her car away. Smith called the police and reported the car stolen. He told Pennsylvania State Police Trooper Elijah Jones that Top Notch had repossessed it on the loan company’s behalf.Stolen-car database entry led to Edwards’s arrest and two weeks in jailTrooper Jones entered the car as stolen in the national CLEAN/NCIC crime database. The entry identified Alburg as its registered owner and recorded that the registered owner had left with the vehicle. Two weeks later, on 17 August 2018, Timothy Edwards was driving the car with Alburg’s permission.Ridley Township Police Officer Timothy Kearney noticed a blue tarp covering the car’s rear window and checked its registration number in the CLEAN database. The search showed that the vehicle had been reported stolen. Kearney stopped the car and arrested Edwards. At the police station, Edwards was charged with receiving stolen property, unauthorised use of a motor vehicle, driving under a suspended licence and driving without a licence. He could not pay the $10,000 bail and remained in jail for two weeks.Police pursued theft charges against Alburg despite title listing her as ownerOn 22 August 2018, Alburg’s lawyer wrote to Jones and Corporal Thomas Falcon, explaining that Alburg owned the car and had permitted Edwards to drive it. He also pointed out that AEL was a secured creditor seeking to recover a debt and that the police had to remain neutral in such disputes. Despite this explanation, Falcon later considered charging Alburg.An assistant district attorney advised that ownership was determined by the vehicle’s title, which listed Alburg as owner and Auto Equity Loans as lienholder. Falcon nevertheless decided that the loan company was the true owner and directed Jones to file a criminal complaint against Alburg.Jones’s complaint described the car as belonging to the company. A magisterial district judge issued an arrest warrant charging Alburg with theft by unlawful taking, theft by deception and unauthorised use of a motor vehicle. She was arrested on 4 February 2019. The Montgomery County Court of Common Pleas later dismissed the theft charges on 22 May 2019 and dropped the unauthorised-use charge on 13 September 2019.Separately, Edwards pleaded guilty to driving with a suspended licence in the Delaware County Court of Common Pleas on 12 February 2019. He was fined $200, while the theft charges against him were dismissed.How did the court assess the police response to the car ownership disputeThe court said police were required to remain neutral in private disputes between creditors and debtors. It found that Jones had sided with the loan company by entering the car as stolen in the national database. However, it granted summary judgment to the officers on Alburg’s claims of illegal seizure and denial of due process. It refused to dismiss her false-arrest and malicious-prosecution claims, finding that disputes over the facts and witnesses’ credibility needed to be resolved.Detective Charles Palo drafted the criminal complaint against Edwards. The court also granted qualified immunity to Jones, Palo, and Kearney on Edwards’s malicious-prosecution claim. It did not make a final ruling on whether the officers were liable to Alburg. Instead, it left the questions of probable cause and the officers’ conduct for further consideration.Disclaimer: This article is based on a memorandum opinion issued by the US District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania on 21 May 2025. The Times of India has not independently verified the facts or allegations presented by the parties. The claims, arguments, and court findings mentioned in this article are reported as recorded in the court opinion.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Russian 'Bears' return to Vietnam after 12 years: Why Moscow's Tu-95 deployment matters
articles.summary: Russia has brought back its nuclear-capable strategic bombers to Vietnam after 12 years, reviving a military arrangement that once allowed Moscow to
articles.body: Russia has brought back its nuclear-capable strategic bombers to Vietnam after 12 years, reviving a military arrangement that once allowed Moscow to operate long-range aircraft in the region.The deployment could bring Russian bombers within striking distance of one of America's most important military bases in the Pacific.According to Reuters report, the two Tu-95 strategic bombers, known to Nato as 'Bears', accompanied by two long-range tanker aircraft, were stationed at Da Nang airport in central Vietnam on Wednesday.The aircraft had flown south from Russia's Far East and arrived in Vietnam on Tuesday, marking Moscow's most significant military aircraft deployment across East Asia in possibly more than a decade.The return of the Tu-95 bombers comes amid heightened military activity near Japan and Taiwan, raising questions about Moscow's ambitions in the Indo-Pacific and the message it wants to send to Beijing.The last known deployment of Russian strategic aircraft to Vietnam took place in 2014, when Hanoi offered Russian warships and military aircraft preferential access to its Cold War-era naval facility at Cam Ranh Bay and the airfield at Da Nang, according to Ian Storey, a security scholar at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute.During that deployment, Russia stationed Il-78 aerial refuelling tankers at Da Nang to support Tu-95 strategic bomber flights near Guam, home to major US air and naval bases in the Pacific.Storey told Reuters that he was unaware of any subsequent deployments and suggested that the operations may have been suspended after the administration of then US President Barack Obama raised concerns with Hanoi.Last year, Moscow sought to revive the arrangement, but Hanoi was initially hesitant, Nguyen The Phuong, a Vietnam security expert at the University of New South Wales in Australia, told Reuters.He said the latest deployment, ostensibly for refuelling, could signal a change in Vietnam's approach and potentially pave the way for further Russian military aircraft deployments.The move is significant for Russia, which has been seeking to maintain its military presence in the Indo-Pacific despite its ongoing war in Ukraine. Access to Vietnamese facilities could provide Moscow with greater operational flexibility for long-range bomber missions across Southeast Asia and the western Pacific.The Tu-95's significance extends beyond its long-range capabilities. The aircraft is a key component of Russia's strategic aviation fleet and can carry nuclear-capable cruise missiles. Its deployment, accompanied by aerial refuelling tankers, demonstrates Moscow's ability to operate strategic aircraft far from its own territory.What message does the deployment send to China?The deployment also carries a message for Beijing, as Vietnam seeks to maintain its strategic balance amid growing Chinese military influence in Southeast Asia.China announced in late September that it was helping Laos build a new military airfield to train its air force. Vietnam has not publicly criticised the move but is monitoring developments to ensure that the facility does not eventually become a military base, Nguyen told Reuters.Hanoi and Beijing are also locked in territorial disputes over parts of the South China Sea. Against this backdrop, Vietnam has often viewed its strong military relationship with Moscow as a strategic counterweight to China.Phuong said Hanoi could have allowed the Russian deployment partly to signal its position to Beijing. Ian Storey said the move could be intended to "signal to China that its military ties to Russia remain strong".The development also highlights the complex relationship between Moscow, Beijing and Hanoi. While Russia and China have strengthened their military and political partnership, Vietnam continues to maintain close defence ties with Moscow to protect its own strategic interests.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Why should Mumbaikars not have such roads?': Bombay high court slams BMC over VIP-only clean-up drives
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The Bombay high court on Wednesday pulled up the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) for sprucing up Mumbai’s roads only during VIP visits,
articles.body: MUMBAI: The Bombay high court on Wednesday pulled up the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) for sprucing up Mumbai’s roads only during VIP visits, questioning why ordinary citizens were denied the same civic upkeep.Hearing a matter related to civic conditions in the city, a division bench of Justices Girish Kulkarni and Neela Gokhale cited the example of south Mumbai’s Ballard Estate, news agency PTI reported.The judges noted that the area had been thoroughly cleaned and its roads washed with water ahead of the arrival of important guests.“Look at Ballard Estate. How shining and polished it is. You have cleaned the streets with water because some important guests have come. Why should Mumbaikars not have such roads?” the court asked the civic body.While the bench did not name the VIP guests, Britain’s Prince William and Princess Catherine, who are currently in the city, had visited Ballard Estate in south Mumbai on Monday.The HC said it was sad that a constitutional court had to deal with the issue of huge amounts of garbage lying on public roads and streets. It added that the BMC could do wonders if it wanted to, PTI reported.“When important people visit the city, the BMC spruces the streets up. Why can’t this be done at all times for the people living in this city? Instead of indulging in such a two-day temporary show that our roads are neat and clean, the BMC can have a permanent show,” the bench remarked.The court said cleanliness should be maintained everywhere and at all times, and not be limited to areas visited by important people, PTI reported.It also urged the civic body and the Maharashtra government to raise awareness about the ill effects of dumping garbage on public streets. The bench asked them to consider stricter implementation of the ban on plastic bags.“We need aggressive campaigns to raise awareness among the general public. Look at the amount of plastic bags strewn on roads. articles.title: Dolly Parton grew up in a small Tennessee cabin and dreamed of leaving a lasting mark on Nashville; weeks after her death, a 240-room hotel and museum spanning over 20,000 square feet opened to visitors
articles.summary: Weeks after Dolly Parton died at the age of 80 in August 2026, the country music star's final Nashville project has opened its doors to the public.
articles.body: Weeks after Dolly Parton died at the age of 80 in August 2026, the country music star's final Nashville project has opened its doors to the public. SongTeller Hotel and Dolly's Life of Many Colors Museum officially welcomed visitors in downtown Nashville on 29 September 2026. The 12-storey building is located one block from Lower Broadway, at 211 Commerce Street and 126 3rd Avenue North. It is a lasting tribute to a woman who grew up in a one-room cabin in East Tennessee before becoming a worldwide music star. Parton died on 25 August 2026 after a short battle with cancer. She had spent years working on the hotel and museum with her longtime Dollywood partner, Herschend, and creative studio AOA. Before her death, she also recorded video and audio messages to guide visitors through the museum galleries. "This museum is a place where folks can see my journey through my own eyes, every color, every story, and every dream that brought me here," Parton said in an official statement released before the opening. "I can't wait to welcome visitors from around the world to Nashville to share in my life of many colors."A 240-room hotel in Music CitySeveral modern country music stars have put their names on bars along Nashville's Lower Broadway. However, Time Out reports that Parton is the first to open a major hotel under her name in the area. According to Time Out and MusicRow, SongTeller Hotel has 240 rooms and suites. Guests can choose from special rooms, including the Six Sisters Suite, which can sleep groups of up to six people, and the two-storey SongTeller Suite. The hotel also has two live music venues and a café. Parton's Live is on the second floor and serves Southern food while hosting songwriter performances. Jolene's is on the top floor and takes its name from Parton's famous 1973 song. Merrill Puckett Miller, chief creative officer at Herschend, called the hotel "Dolly's love letter to Nashville," according to travel publication Deep Arrival. Parton personally chose the former office building near Lower Broadway, even though it was not officially for sale at the time.Inside Dolly's Life of Many Colors MuseumThe museum takes up the entire third floor of the building. Dolly's Life of Many Colors Museum covers more than 20,000 square feet and includes around 20 rooms designed to give visitors an experience of Parton's life. According to its official website, it is the largest exhibition about her life anywhere in the world. For the opening, curators brought together more than 300 personal items and almost 300 pieces of historical video footage. Visitors enter through a separate entrance at street level on 3rd Avenue North. They then follow a timeline that begins on 19 January 1946, the night Parton was born. The first galleries show what her childhood home in the Smoky Mountains looked like. They also include a copy of the patchwork coat her mother made for her. That coat later inspired Parton's 1971 song Coat of Many Colors. Other rooms explore her songwriting, including a recreation of her writing room.Visitors can also see a copy of her custom tour bus, which represents her years on the road, and seven decades of stage costumes. Steve Summers, Parton's longtime creative director and costume designer, told travel magazine AFAR that her lifelong friend Judy Ogle helped make it possible to save so many items from her early career. "Because of Judy Ogle, Dolly saved everything," Summers said. He explained that Parton was not as interested in owning things as she was in helping visitors understand her love of songwriting, performing and her fans.Rediscovered keepsakes and global literacyOne of the most personal items in the museum is the short, white A-line dress Parton wore when she married Carl Dean in Ringgold, Georgia, in May 1966. Parton had believed the dress was lost for many years. According to Noelle Nashville and Wedded Wonderland, her niece and museum executive director, Rebecca Seaver, found it in 2024. The dress was inside a paper grocery bag, which had been placed in a military trunk that once belonged to Dean. The trunk also held her wedding veil, the Bible she carried during the ceremony, a letter from the pastor who married the couple and photo booth pictures of the two that had never been seen before. Dean died in March 2025 at the age of 82. Another gallery tells the story of the Imagination Library, Parton's book charity, which she started in 1995 in memory of her father. He had been unable to read. According to the museum's official website, the programme has given away more than 300 million free books to children around the world. "Dolly's Life of Many Colors Museum is the largest collection of Dolly's life story we have ever displayed," Seaver said in official opening materials quoted by Deep Arrival.Visiting the Nashville landmarkThe museum is open every day from 9am to 5pm. Visitors can buy timed-entry tickets through its website. General admission starts at $29.99. Children aged five and under can enter free when accompanied by an adult who has paid for a ticket. There are also two shops selling official merchandise at the property. One is on the ground floor and is open to everyone. The other is a boutique that can only be visited by people with museum tickets.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US court halts restrictions on internships for foreign students; CPT relief for universities
articles.summary: In a relief to international students pursuing higher education in the US, a district court (Massachusetts) has blocked the enforcement of restrictions
articles.body: In a relief to international students pursuing higher education in the US, a district court (Massachusetts) has blocked the enforcement of restrictions introduced by the Trump administration on curricular practical training (CPT), which allows foreign students on F-1 visas to undertake internships and practical training linked to their academic programmes.The district court, in an order dated Nov 17, stayed two policy broadcasts issued by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) in August 2026, pending judicial review. The order also restrains the government from implementing the broadcasts’ interpretation of CPT requirements against the plaintiffs and their members, including their employees and students.The dispute arose after SEVP issued broadcasts on Aug 12 and Aug 24, effectively narrowing eligibility for CPT. Under the revised interpretation, practical training would qualify only if it was mandatory for all students pursuing a particular degree programme. This excluded elective internships and training undertaken for academic credit, even where such opportunities formed part of a student’s curriculum.The change represented a departure from the federal government’s longstanding position dating back to 1991, under which elective training undertaken for academic credit could qualify as CPT.The district court observed that the government had changed its interpretation without acknowledging or explaining the departure from its earlier position. It held that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in their challenge arguing that the change was arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.“SEVP departed from its longstanding position of treating elective for-credit training as CPT without acknowledging, let alone explaining, the change or considering serious reliance interests,” Judge Julia E. Kobick stated.Universities had been forced to respond to the Aug broadcasts by withdrawing or denying CPT approvals, revising curricula and altering career guidance for students. Columbia University, for instance, told the court it had denied CPT authorisation to more than 120 international students for the fall semester. At Grinnell College, at least 13 students lost internship opportunities. Others like Cornell and Michigan State University, said they have already lost students because of the broadcasts.The district court noted that some institutions had lost students because of the restrictions, while designated school officials (DSOs) faced increased stress and apprehension about potential personal liability for approving training that could be viewed as non-compliant.The plaintiffs—including the Association of American Universities, Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, and NAFSA: Association of International Educators—had argued that the policy change disrupted students’ academic and career plans and imposed substantial costs on universities.Granting interim relief, the court said the institutions had demonstrated irreparable harm, including expenditure of substantial resources to comply with the broadcasts and the threat of losing certification to enrol international students.The order stays the Aug12 and Aug 24 broadcasts nationwide pending judicial review. Separately, the preliminary injunction prohibits the defendants from implementing or enforcing the new interpretation against the plaintiffs and their members, including students and employees, both prospectively and in relation to conduct and approvals predating the broadcasts.You use AI every day. articles.summary: VISAKHAPATNAM: The Cyclone Akvan intensified into a severe cyclonic storm over the central parts of the south and adjoining west-central Bay of Bengal on
articles.body: VISAKHAPATNAM: The Cyclone Akvan intensified into a severe cyclonic storm over the central parts of the south and adjoining west-central Bay of Bengal on Wednesday morning.The severe cyclonic storm is crawling towards Andhra Pradesh and it is likely to cross north Andhra Pradesh and Yanam and south Odisha coasts between Narsapur and Puri, by November 20 as a severe cyclonic storm with the maximum sustained wind speed of 90-100kmph gusting to 110kmph.The impacts in Andhra Pradesh are very likely to be in the form of extremely heavy rainfall accompanied by strong gales in six coastal districts, heavy to very heavy rainfall accompanied by winds in six districts, and heavy rainfall in four districts.Authorities in parts of the north coastal Andhra Pradesh have stepped up precautionary measures ahead of the cyclone, they may shift residents of vulnerable and structurally unsafe homes in the region to designated shelters.Some senior officials were deployed for overall supervision of preparedness, relief and restoration measures.The cyclone Akvan over westcentral and adjoining central parts of south Bay of Bengal was moving north-northwestwards at slow speed and it lay centred over the same region about 520km southeast of Narsapur (Andhra Pradesh), 560km east of Chennai (Tamil Nadu), 570km south-southeast of Kalingapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), 660km south of Gopalpur (Odisha) and 720km south of Puri (Odisha).The slow speed gives the system time to gain momentum over warm water.IMD on Wednesday morning forecast that the cyclone would cross land between Nellore and Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh.It altered the forecast in the afternoon, saying the landfall would be between Narsapur and Puri.The weather agency expects Akvan to cross the north Andhra Pradesh and Yanam and south Odisha coasts on Friday (November 20) noon. The crossing point is likely to be between Narsapur and Puri as a severe cyclonic storm with the maximum sustained wind speed of 90-100kmph gusting to 110kmph.The intensity forecast has been brought down a notch. Initially IMD predicted that the system may landfall as a very severe cyclonic storm, but now expects the landfall as a severe cyclonic storm, not the very severe storm it projected earlier.Winds of 90-100kmph, gusting up to 110kmph, are expected from Thursday (November 19) night until landfall on Friday, November 20, noon.Heavy To Extremely RainsThe IMD has issued a red alert (extremely heavy rainfall prediction) for six districts- Kakinada, Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, Alluri Sitharama Raju (ASR), and Ankapalle and Yanam of Union Territory of Puducherry for Thursday (November 19).It has issued an orange alert (heavy to very heavy rainfall) for Parvathipuram Manyam, West Godavari, East Godavari and Konaseema districts for Thursday.Heavy rainfall is likely at one or two places over Eluru, Krishna, Guntur, and Bapatla districts on Thursday. Gale winds speed reaching 90-100kmph gusting up to 110kmph likely at isolated places Coastal Andhra Pradesh, Yanam.Six districts Kakinada, Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, Ankapalle and Parvathipuram Manyam and Yanam are covered by the red alert for Friday (November 20), and orange alert for ASR and Konaseema districts, and isolated heavy rainfall over Eluru, Krishna, Guntur, Bapatla, East Godavari, and West Godavari districts for the same day as well.Gale winds speed reaching 90-100kmph gusting up to 110kmph likely at isolated places Coastal Andhra Pradesh, Yanam.IMD has forecast isolated heavy rainfall over Kakinada, Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, ASR, Anakapalle, and Manyam districts on Saturday (November 21).You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Visakhapatnam | Silver Rate in Visakhapatnam | Bank Holidays in Visakhapatnam | Public Holidays in Visakhapatnam | Petrol Price in Visakhapatnam | Diesel Price in Visakhapatnam | CNG Price in Visakhapatnam | LPG Price in VisakhapatnamStay updated with the latest Visakhapatnam news. articles.body: Drake has entered the Grand Theft Auto 6 excitement after calling streamer Adin Ross to question how he managed to access the game before its official release. During their November 18 conversation, the two discussed the New Zealand trick, which players are trying to use to play early. The discussion soon turned into a bet, with Ross asking Drake for his unreleased song Piece of Me if he won.Drake challenges Adin Ross over the GTA 6 New Zealand trickThe conversation took place during Adin Ross’ livestream, when Drake called the streamer after hearing that he had supposedly found a way to play GTA 6 before its November 19 launch. The rapper wanted to understand how Ross had managed to get access to one of the most awaited video games of the year.Ross explained that he could use a New Zealand account to access the game earlier. The method is based on time differences between countries. Since New Zealand reaches midnight before many other parts of the world, players sometimes change their account region to access games when they become available there.However, Drake was not ready to believe that the method would work. Instead of accepting Ross’ explanation, he challenged the streamer to prove it.Drake said, “You would not be able to get the game running within 45 minutes.”Ross accepted the challenge and remained confident that he could make it happen. He then saw an opportunity to ask the rapper for something more valuable than money. If his method worked, he wanted Drake to send him the complete version of his unreleased track Piece of Me.This turned their conversation into an unusual wager, bringing together the excitement around GTA 6 and interest in Drake’s unreleased music.Adin Ross’ GTA 6 unboxing drama and Drake’s radio station rumoursThis is not the first time Adin Ross has attracted attention over his attempts to get GTA 6 before its official launch. On November 13, the streamer claimed that he had paid $10,000 for an early copy of the game. Viewers reportedly claimed that someone watching the broadcast had redeemed it before he could use it. articles.title: US used expired missiles in Op Epic Fury against Iran; navy officer gives odd 'stale bread' comparison
articles.summary: A bottle of medicine past its expiry date is usually thrown away. But what happens when the weapon meant to destroy an enemy target is past its shelf life?
articles.body: A bottle of medicine past its expiry date is usually thrown away. But what happens when the weapon meant to destroy an enemy target is past its shelf life?The US navy faced precisely that question during its war against Iran, where it brought expired munitions back into service, exposing a growing strain on America's military stockpiles.The disclosure came from acting navy secretary Hung Cao during his confirmation hearing before the Senate Armed Services Committee on Tuesday.Responding to questions from Senator Deb Fischer on whether the navy was striking the right balance between expensive precision-guided weapons and cheaper, mass-produced munitions, Cao revealed that the navy had recoded previously expired weapons to make them fit for use during Operation Epic Fury against Iran.He said some of the munitions had been classified under Code Echo and Code Foxtrot, indicating that they were expired or unserviceable.Explaining how the navy brought the weapons back into service, Cao said the munitions had been recoded after being classified as expired.He compared the process to reviving stale bread, saying, "I came from a poor family, right? You know, bread, things like bread doesn't expire. You just rub some water on, microwave for 15 seconds, and it's good to go."He added, "For some of these munitions, we recoded them, and so we're able to shoot off the expired munitions."However, Cao did not disclose how many such weapons were used, which specific missile systems were involved or what technical inspections were carried out before they were cleared for combat.The distinction matters because crossing a prescribed shelf life does not automatically make a missile unsafe, but its continued use requires technical assessment and certification.Cao also sought to reassure lawmakers that the navy was expanding its weapons production capacity to address the pressure on its stockpiles.Citing the Tomahawk cruise missile programme, he said annual production had risen sharply from the levels during his military career. "When I was in uniform, we only produced 125 Tomahawks a year. Right now we're well above 60 every month," he told the committee.He added that the navy was working with defence manufacturers to increase production of SM-6 missiles, while bringing new companies into the munitions supply chain.Why using expired weapons is a risky gambleUsing expired munitions in combat can turn a precision strike into an unpredictable gamble. Missiles rely on a combination of propellants, explosives, electronic guidance systems and mechanical components, all of which can deteriorate during prolonged storage.As these materials age, the risk of malfunction increases, potentially affecting a weapon's ability to launch, reach its intended target or detonate on impact.According to the United Nations' Manual on Ammunition Management, ageing ammunition can undergo chemical changes, including the depletion of stabilising compounds in propellants, deterioration of explosive materials and corrosion of components.In solid-fuel missiles, cracks in the propellant can alter the burning process, potentially causing abnormal pressure and affecting thrust. Deterioration of electronic components can also compromise navigation and guidance, while ageing fuzes may prevent a warhead from detonating as intended.The risks are not limited to a failed strike. Unstable or degraded ammunition can also pose hazards during storage, handling, transportation and launch. A missile that malfunctions may fail to reach its target, detonate prematurely or remain unexploded, potentially leaving dangerous explosive material behind.Retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, has explained that expiry dates are intended to account for the increasing likelihood of technical problems as missiles age. Older weapons can, however, be returned to service after appropriate inspections and technical assessments establish that they remain reliable.

articles.title: A Missouri university employee won $631,000 for a hostile work environment and additional damages over her departure; an appeals court preserved the $631,000 award but ordered a retrial of the separate damages
articles.summary: A Missouri appeals court has upheld a jury's finding that Lincoln University subjected a former employee to a racially hostile work environment, while
articles.body: A Missouri appeals court has upheld a jury's finding that Lincoln University subjected a former employee to a racially hostile work environment, while overturning the damages awarded on her separate constructive discharge claim and ordering a fresh trial limited to those damages.The Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District, issued its ruling on November 17 in the case involving Sheila Gassner, a former university employee who alleged that she was discriminated against because she was white. The court affirmed the judgment in her favour on the hostile work environment claim but reversed the actual and punitive damages awarded for constructive discharge.The case has been sent back to the circuit court for a new trial on damages related to the constructive discharge claim. The appeals court also granted Gassner's request for attorney fees incurred during the appeal.Employee alleged excessive workload, unequal payGassner joined Lincoln University in 1989 and became director of design and construction in 1999. In November 2013, after the university terminated its director of buildings and grounds, its president and chief of staff asked her to take over those responsibilities in addition to her existing duties.She was reassigned as executive director for facilities and planning, effectively overseeing two departments. Her salary was increased to $79,000, just 1.8 per cent more than what she had earned in her earlier position.According to the court ruling, her workload nearly doubled, forcing her to work between 70 and 80 hours a week. She also had to manage more than 40 employees and handle round-the-clock emergency responsibilities.Gassner repeatedly raised concerns about her workload and compensation. However, university officials allegedly told her that a budget crisis prevented them from increasing her salary or providing additional staff.During the same period, the university created three executive positions and appointed African-American men without advertising the vacancies. Several African-American employees also received salary increases ranging from 12.5% to 44.5%, despite some having fewer responsibilities and working fewer hours than Gassner.The university's former human resources director testified that funds were available through the president's contingency fund and that the explanation about a budget crisis was inaccurate.Gassner resigned in June 2018, saying her working conditions had become intolerable. She subsequently filed a discrimination complaint and sued the university under the Missouri Human Rights Act.Appeals court reverses part of damages awardA jury ruled in Gassner's favour in December 2024, awarding her $131,000 in actual damages and $500,000 in punitive damages for the hostile work environment claim.For the constructive discharge claim, the jury awarded her $110,000 in back pay, $30,000 in non-economic damages and $500,000 in punitive damages. The trial court later reduced the punitive damages on this claim to $170,000.The university challenged the verdict, arguing, among other things, that Gassner's claims were time-barred and that the jury had been incorrectly instructed on damages.The appeals court rejected the university's arguments concerning the time limits, finding that Gassner had presented evidence of a continuing pattern of alleged discrimination. It also upheld the trial court's decision to exclude an unsigned draft of her resignation letter, ruling that it was protected by attorney-client privilege.However, the court found an error in the instructions given to the jury on the university's defence that Gassner had failed to mitigate her losses by seeking other employment.The trial court had required the university to establish additional conditions beyond those prescribed under Missouri's standard jury instruction. This placed a higher evidentiary burden on the university, the appeals court said.The judges noted that the jury had awarded Gassner the full $110,000 in back pay sought by her lawyer, even though she had not pursued certain employment opportunities after leaving the university.Consequently, the court reversed the actual damages award on the constructive discharge claim. Since actual damages must be awarded before punitive damages can be granted, it also overturned the $170,000 punitive damages award on that claim.The court ordered a new trial limited to damages for constructive discharge, with the jury to receive the correct instructions on failure to mitigate damages.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tynwald members to privately view unredacted windfarm documents
articles.summary: Tynwald members will privately view the unredacted agreements for the Mooir Vannin Wind Farm.
articles.body:
Tynwald members will have the opportunity to privately view the unredacted agreements for the Mooir Vannin Wind Farm.

The proposals could see 87 turbines built six to 12 miles (11.1km to 22.2km) off the eastern coast from Maughold.

It comes after Garff MHK Richard Henthorn withdrew a motion in the court on Tuesday calling for its publication prior to the issue being debated at next month's sitting.

Redacted versions of the agreements will be placed on the Tynwald Register of Business which members of the public can view.

The documents, which were created to support the development of the proposed wind farm, remain subject to marine infrastructure consent.

A recommendation report from an independent examining body is also due to be submitted to the Council of Ministers at the start of December.

Infrastructure Minister Jason Moorhouse confirmed the lease by the department, Dong Energy Isle of Man and Dong Energy Wind Power A/S, as well as an Amendment to the Agreement for Lease, are to be released to "a secure reading room for private viewing".

Taking to Facebook on Wednesday, Henthorn posted: "I can now use the information within this document to take to further debates on the subject."

At the sitting, he also called for a general debate on government policy for using seabed rental to achieve revenue.

He pointed out that the island has not yet completed a marine spatial plan for the seabed and urged for the work to take place before any agreements are made.

"Government must have the marine spatial plan before we go any further, we need to know if the seabed is work more than what is being offered and we should know before any consent is granted," he said.

Arbory, Castletown and Malew MHK, Kirree Jenkins added the plan is just one part of the answer, it does not tell members what the value of the seabed is.

And Gary Clueit MLC produced a series of questions to be asked ahead of any seabed applications.

Among others, he asked government to question what the financial return would be to the government, what rights the island would retain and how much economic activity would remain on the island.

articles.title: During WWII, Gunner Norman Ellor filmed a cheeky love message for his fiancée in Burma; decades later, their sons watched it alongside the couple’s wartime letters and journals
articles.summary: Explore the romantic wartime message from Gunner Norman Ellor to his fiancée Betty, as their sons discover heartfelt letters and journals offering deeper insights into their parents' enduring love during WWII.
articles.body: Once, a British soldier stood before a camera, bare-chested, and delivered a message for the woman who was waiting for him at home. Gunner Norman Ellor began his message saying, “Betty darling, you’ve often said in your letters that you’d like to see me.Well, here I am.” He then cheekily added that he hoped she was sitting in the front row and would get a good look at him. Norman ended his message by expressing how much he loved her. This playful recording was a part of a wartime effort to connect the British troops who were serving overseas. Decades after the message was recorded, Norman and Betty’s sons watched the video and explored a collection of their parents’ wartime love letters and journals. Those correspondences showcase the depth behind their father’s light-hearted performance.A message for the woman waiting at homeAccording to Channel 4, Norman and Betty had known each other since they were very young and became engaged shortly before he left for Burma. At the time, communications between families living in Britain and the soldiers serving overseas were extremely difficult. One such option for communication was letters; however, those travelled slowly, and some never arrived. In addition to that, home leave was not easily available for the troops serving in the Far East; thus, many were unable to see their loved ones for years.This filmed message from Norman offered Betty a chance to see him after ages rather than simply reading his words. In his short address, he spoke directly to her and joked about his appearance. The recording belonged to Calling Blighty, a series of short films made between 1944 and 1946 by the Directorate of Army Welfare in India. To improve morale among the servicemen, this project was initiated. Camera crews filmed soldiers delivering personal messages, which were then sent back to their towns and communities. Families and friends were invited to watch the footage at special screenings in local cinemas.According to Channel 4, 391 films were produced. Each of them lasted around 10-15 minutes and featured approximately 8,000 men and a small number of women. The North West Film Archive reported that soldiers usually delivered the messages while looking straight at the camera, and often in a single take.The letters exchanged between them showcased a different side of NormanYears following the Second World War, their sons, Steve and Rob Ellor, discovered a collection of love letters and journals that belonged to their parents. The documents offered a more private account of Norman’s experience in the war. While his on-camera message was cheeky and affectionate, his wartime writings shed light on how much he missed home and how difficult it was for him to continue fighting.Furthermore, the correspondence revealed that the separation sometimes placed pressure on their relationship. According to their son Steve, Norman began referring to jealousy in his letters as the distance continued. Steve also described his mother as a lifeline for his father throughout his time in the Army. Therefore, these letters contributed more context to the filmed message.A marriage that survived separationThe wartime separation did not prevent the couple from building the life that they had hoped for. Betty waited for Norman to return home, and they got married just 10 days later under a special licence. Channel 4 describes their subsequent marriage as a long, happy one. Meanwhile, for their sons, seeing the decades-old footage offered a rare glimpse of their father as a young man looking into the camera and speaking to the woman he one day hoped to marry. Rob described watching it as looking through a time capsule into the 1940s.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Exciting' £7.5m Rutland County Museum revamp given green light
articles.summary: The council aims to turn Rutland County Museum into a "first-class visitor attraction".
articles.body:
Plans to turn Rutland County Museum into a "first-class visitor attraction" have been given the green light.

The £7.5m renovation of the Grade II listed-museum, in Catmos Street, Oakham, will include a new extension to house a multi-purpose hall, cafe, shop and new galleries.

The project will also include digital interpretations of the Rutland Sea Dragon - which was unearthed in 2021 - and the Ketton Roman Mosaic , discovered in 2020.

Rutland County Council said the redevelopment, which was approved by its planning committee on Tuesday, was "exciting" and designed to secure the museum's long-term future.

The Liberal Democrat-led authority said the renovation would also include repairs and improvements to existing listed buildings, a new Stone Age to Medieval Gallery and accessible improvements, such as a new platform lift.

Enhancements to the surrounding grounds and South Street car park will also be carried out as well as environmental improvements, including energy efficiency measures, solar panels on the new extension, sustainable drainage and additional native tree planting.

The existing non-listed poultry hall is set to be demolished to allow other buildings to be extended.

The Rutland Sea Dragon - a 180-million-year-old ichthyosaur - was initially earmarked to be displayed following the renovation of the museum.

However, plans to display the fossil - which was found on the shore of Rutland Water in 2021 - were abandoned by the council in May , after estimated costs rose by £1m.

The authority said the project would be funded by £6m from the council and £1.5m of local regeneration funding from the government.

Council leader Christine Wise previously said the renovation was "hugely exciting" and would preserve the museum "long into the future by turning it into a first-class visitor attraction" and multi-use community space.

Rosemary Powell, portfolio holder for economy and place at the council, said: "This is an exciting step forward for Rutland County Museum and a significant investment in the future of our county's heritage and culture.

"Our museum plays an important role in telling the story of Rutland, bringing our history to life and providing opportunities for people of all ages to learn, explore and enjoy our collections.

"These plans will help us protect and celebrate the historic buildings while creating the additional space and facilities needed to make the museum an even more welcoming and accessible place to visit.

"The new exhibition areas, multi-purpose hall and cafe will also open up opportunities for more activities, events and community experiences."

She added that the redevelopment was also about "creating a vibrant, welcoming destination" for people to visit Oakham.

Work to renovate Rutland County Museum is due to start in March and will be completed later in 2027.

articles.title: Kenya halted eight baobabs from being shipped to Georgia after a licensing outcry in 2022; the export later went ahead in 2023, and all eight trees died
articles.summary: The export of eight baobabs from Kenya to Georgia faced controversy over environmental permits and local community impact, resulting in the death of all trees shortly after their relocation.
articles.body: Kenya’s export of eight adult baobabs to Georgia sparked debate on conservation, local community interests, and biological resource trade. The Baobabs were dug out of their homes in Kenya's coastal Kilifi County for a botanical park that was associated with Bidzina Ivanishvili, the outgoing prime minister of Georgia. In November 2022, the government suspended the export, citing a lack of necessary permits and approval, but eventually, permission was granted. On August 24, it was confirmed that the eight trees were dead, illustrating the risk of moving giant trees across the world.How the export plan triggered an outcry The controversy broke out after contractors began buying mature trees for villages in Mtondia and Tezo in Kilifi County. The Guardian reported that the offers ranged from 100,000 to 300,000 Kenyan shillings for each mature baobab. Farmers in the largely poor community hailed the money, which earned them a well-paying living, but conservationists questioned whether the relevant permits had been obtained, and whether the National Environment Management Authority and the Kenya Forest Service had issued approval. The Health Inspector Service, which issued the export permit, was also involved when the environmental authority letter asked whether the necessary procedures had been followed.In November 2022, President William Ruto directed the Ministry of Environment and Forestry to investigate how the licence was being issued. The transportation of the eight trees was halted by the Ministry, and the Environment CS, Soipan Tuya, told the media that the environmental impact assessment licence was obtained illegally. The government also pointed out that it was important to comply with the Nagoya Protocol, which sets out the guidelines and the regulations for genetic material through prior informed consent and fair and equitable benefit sharing. This was not a final stop for the movement of the trees. In August 2023, the Kenyan Senate was told that the export was initially interrupted because the concerned agencies had to conclude that the procedures had not been followed. The project officials were later contacted, and it was found that compliance was in order, and the export was then allowed.Why the trees were moved and what happened in GeorgiaThe eight baobabs were destined for Shekvetili Dendrological Park, on Georgia’s Black Sea coast. The park opened to visitors in 2020 and brought trees and other plants from across the globe. The export drew attention because of the park’s link to Ivanishvili, Georgia’s prime minister in 2012-13. Mature trees must be excavated, and some roots are often severed or damaged. This requires some amount of effort to take out a tree, and even the most robust trees can be under stress if the process is drawn out.The parks administration later explained what took place. The trees had actually been uprooted in 2021. But did not reach Georgia until October 2023. The trees were planted on 8 November that year, by which time they had been out of the ground for nearly two years and had actually been badly kept, in declining health. They died after 6 to 7 months. The problem was the holdup of the project that took so long.What the deaths mean for baobab conservationEight trees down, and the ecological and cultural significance of baobabs is once again in the spotlight. The dam has eight giant baobabs native to sub-Saharan Africa. Leaves, fruit, and bark have value, and the tree’s iconic bottle-shaped trunk stores water and allows it to thrive in a dry environment with seasonal rainfall. Research published in Environmental Management examined baobabs in a 15-square-kilometre area in Kenya. It identified 432 trees in a 2,015-square-kilometre area and noted the significance of species to households, such as providing food and other available resources. It also highlighted issues with regeneration of the trees and why the death of the biggest and most mature baobab trees was much more significant than the death of an individual tree.This episode illustrated the importance of open licensing and informed community consultation. While the benefits of getting trees to the market may bring immediate financial returns, ensuring the local communities understand their long-term benefits is as critical as completing export paperwork. The loss of trees may not necessarily mean that the prospect of international translocation of baobabs is not possible. It is a demonstration of the kind of risk that is involved in removing plants without undertaking the proper planning and looking for the right growing conditions.You use AI every day. articles.title: Two Missouri property owners tried to sell for $272,500, but former sellers refused to clear a mortgage that was paid off; the deal collapsed, the property later sold for $225,000 and a court upheld $47,500 in damages
articles.summary: A property deal worth $272,500 fell through after a Missouri couple could not get a mortgage released that they said had already been paid off.
articles.body: A property deal worth $272,500 fell through after a Missouri couple could not get a mortgage released that they said had already been paid off. The former sellers refused to drop their financial claim on the property, insisting that some payments were still owed. A court has now backed a $47,500 damages award against them. The Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District, ruled on November 17, 2026, that the evidence backed the original decision in favor of Joseph C. Barber and Brenda L. Barber. The court found that Kimberly R. Weger had no valid financial reason to block the sale after the loan had been paid off. The ruling also upheld a separate legal penalty of $3,732.50, plus $28,065.77 in legal fees and court costs. The appeals court also sent the case back to the lower court to decide on extra legal fees from the appeal. The fight centered on a property at 4905 West Route F in Clark, Missouri, and focused on a dispute over payments made almost ten years before the planned sale.Property purchase and original mortgage agreementAccording to the court's opinion in Joseph C. Barber and Brenda L. Barber v. Kimberly R. Weger, the Barbers bought the property from Kimberly Weger and her husband, Aubrey Weger, in 2006. The buyers signed a loan agreement for $37,325 to cover part of the purchase price. A deed of trust was also filed in favor of the Wegers on November 22, 2006, giving them a legal claim over the property until the loan was paid in full. Under the terms, the Barbers had to pay $450 a month toward the loan and interest. Payments started on December 1, 2006, and ran until November 2015, when the loan ended. The deal also included a $25 late fee if a monthly payment arrived after the 15th of the month. Brenda Barber later testified that the couple made all the required payments, including any late fees. She said they believed the debt was completely settled.$272,500 sale put on holdIn April 2022, the Barbers signed a deal to sell the property for $272,500. The closing date was set for May 13 of that year. Before the sale could close, they learned that the deed of trust in favor of the Wegers was still listed against the property. The former sellers refused to clear it, saying they had not received every monthly payment, especially those from 2014 and 2015. They also refused to give a final payoff figure showing how much they thought was still owed. The court's account notes that Aubrey told Brenda she "couldn't sell the Property" because the Barbers "didn't own it". He also said he would "stop the sale" because he "really wish[ed] they had the house and property back." Their son, Ashtin Weger, also told Brenda that he "would do whatever it took and make sure people knew [the Plaintiffs] didn't own [the Property] and couldn't sell it", because he wanted his "parents to have" the property. The Barbers pushed back the closing date three times and dropped the sale price to $225,000 to try to save the deal. The original sale still collapsed because the deed of trust remained on the record.Legal demand failed to secure mortgage releaseAfter the refusal, the Barbers hired a lawyer to get the deed of trust removed. On May 5, 2022, their lawyer sent an official demand letter under Section 443.130 of Missouri law. It asked the Wegers to sign and file a release document and either return the canceled loan agreement or sign a sworn statement confirming the debt was paid. The letter included bank records showing most of the payments made in 2014 and 2015. The Barbers explained that some older receipts were missing because almost seven years had passed and several payments were made by money order. They also sent money for the filing fees and prepared the forms for the Wegers to sign. The first letter came back after the Wegers refused to accept it. The Barbers' lawyer then sent the same papers through the Wegers' attorney. The buyers also offered to put any disputed money into a secure holding account so the sale could go ahead. The Wegers still refused to give a payoff amount or release the deed of trust. The Barbers then filed a lawsuit in Boone County Circuit Court on August 19, 2022.Former sellers disputed payment recordsDuring the trial, Brenda maintained that she and Joseph made every payment owed under the loan. She explained that they did not save every receipt because they thought the loan was finished. Once the Wegers questioned the payments, she reached out to banks to find old records. The banks could not find proof for six monthly payments from 2014 and 2015. Even so, the Barbers showed the records they were able to get. Kimberly told a different story. She testified that her records showed only 67 of the 107 required payments were made, leaving $17,079.97 unpaid, not counting late fees. She also said she still had the payment records despite a 2017 house fire. According to her testimony, the home office where she kept the files was the only room that did not burn. Kimberly said she did not mean to block the sale and claimed she could not force Aubrey to sign the release. She also testified that she would forgive the unpaid balance if she got a right-of-way agreement across the property. That deal never happened.Court finds refusal to release deed unjustifiedIn June 2024, the trial judge issued a partial ruling ordering the deed of trust to be cleared. The remaining claims for money damages were handled separately. Once the legal hold was lifted, the Barbers finally sold the property for $225,000 on September 16, 2024. In May 2025, the Boone County Circuit Court ruled in their favor on the remaining claims. It granted them $3,732.50 under Missouri's mortgage-release law, plus $28,065.77 in legal fees and court costs. The court also awarded $47,500 for wrongfully interfering with a real estate sale.Kimberly appealed, claiming there was not enough proof that the loan was paid off or that her refusal to release the deed was unfair. The Missouri Court of Appeals turned down both arguments. In its November 17 opinion, the appeals court said the trial judge had the right to believe Brenda's testimony and the bank records as proof that the payments were finished. It also noted that the trial judge was responsible for deciding which witnesses were believable.The judges also ruled that a lender's financial claim on a deed of trust ends as soon as the debt is paid in full. The court noted that the Wegers refused to give a payoff figure despite repeated requests. It also looked at evidence showing their refusal was driven by a wish to stop the Barbers from selling the property because they wanted it back. The appeals judges decided that the refusal was not backed by a valid financial interest.Additional legal fees to be decidedThe court upheld the original ruling, including the $47,500 damages award and the statutory payment. It also approved the Barbers' request for extra legal fees built up after the first ruling and during the appeal. Instead of setting the amount itself, the Missouri Court of Appeals sent the case back to the Boone County Circuit Court to figure out fair post-judgment and appeal legal costs. The November 17 ruling was issued in case WD88284, with Judges Cynthia L. Martin, Lisa White Hardwick, and Gary D. Witt serving on the panel. The decision leaves the $47,500 award standing and requires Kimberly Weger to face another review of the Barbers' legal bills.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Maharashtra deputy chief minister Eknath Shinde on Wednesday backed party spokesperson Shaina NC amid a row over allegations that she tore a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Maharashtra deputy chief minister Eknath Shinde on Wednesday backed party spokesperson Shaina NC amid a row over allegations that she tore a photograph of Bal Thackeray. The Shiv Sena chief clarified, saying "Balasaheb is like a deity to us" and that the torn portion of the picture showed Congress leader Mani Shankar Aiyar's face.Shinde said he had personally seen the photograph and that Shaina had already clarified the matter, news agency ANI reported."Balasaheb Thackeray is like a deity to us. Any insult to him is absolutely unacceptable. No one is permitted to do so. Shaina NC has already provided a clarification. The photograph in question shows Balasaheb Thackeray, who once took to the streets to strike Mani Shankar Aiyar with a slipper for insulting Swatantryaveer Savarkar. The part that was torn in the image was the face of Mani Shankar Aiyar. I have seen it myself," Shinde said.He added that any act of disrespect towards Balasaheb Thackeray would not be tolerated.Shinde also accused Congress leader Sonia Gandhi's memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, of insulting Hindutva ideologue VD Savarkar. He criticised Rahul Gandhi for repeatedly targeting Savarkar and condemned those who, he said, had abandoned Bal Thackeray's ideology."In a book written by Sonia Gandhi, Swatantryaveer Savarkar has been insulted. The Shiv Sena has expressed its protest by tearing out the two offensive pages. Rahul Gandhi repeatedly defames Savarkar, a man who endured such immense suffering and hardship for his country," he said."I condemn Rahul Gandhi for deliberately insulting Savarkar, and I also condemn those who sit alongside him in government, working in close alliance with him. I denounce those who have abandoned the ideology of Balasaheb Thackeray. Anyone who insults Swatantryaveer Savarkar will face condemnation, protest and agitation," he added.A controversy erupted earlier in the day after the Shinde-led Shiv Sena protested against the distribution of Sonia Gandhi's memoir, alleging that it contained objectionable references to Savarkar.Party leaders, including Shaina NC, Sanjay Nirupam and Anand Dubey, tore pages from the book and demanded that publisher HarperCollins remove the passages on pages 201 and 443.The Congress and Shiv Sena (UBT) subsequently accused Shaina of tearing a photograph of Bal Thackeray during the press conference.Shaina rejected the allegation, claiming that the photograph was of Mani Shankar Aiyar and not Bal Thackeray.She also challenged the leaders to prove the allegation and threatened legal action over what she called defamatory claims.Congress Nana Patole, meanwhile, described the incident as "petty, low-level politics" and demanded an FIR, strict action and an apology.Uddhav Sena's Sanjay Raut said Shaina should be "publically flogged" for damaging Balasaheb's photo.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: Vijayawada Municipal Corporation inspects city eateries for hygiene lapses, issues notices, and warns of legal action or trade licence cancellation for non-compliance.
articles.body: Vijayawada: The Vijayawada Municipal Corporation (VMC) has intensified inspections of hotels and restaurants across the city after finding violations of hygiene and food safety norms. Acting on the instructions of in-charge municipal commissioner A Ravindra Rao, public health officials inspected several hotels in Gunadala and One Town on Wednesday.During the inspections, officials found unhygienic conditions at Star Hotel in One Town, Asif Chicken Centre in Urmila Nagar and Subhani Hotel in Gunadala, among other establishments. The violations included fungal growth on walls and other surfaces, poor maintenance of premises, use of unsafe drinking water and improperly maintained toilets.Officials also found food being prepared and business operations being carried out in unhygienic surroundings, raising concerns over public health and food safety.The civic body issued notices to the hotel managements where violations were detected and directed them to rectify the deficiencies within the stipulated time. The establishments have been asked to comply with hygiene, sanitation and food safety requirements.Officials warned that failure to address the violations within the deadline would invite further legal action, including possible cancellation of trade licences. articles.title: India at COP31: Developing countries cannot be made to bear burden of rich nations’ historical emissions
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India said on Wednesday that the Global South (developing countries) cannot be made to bear the burden of historical emissions in the name of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India said on Wednesday that the Global South (developing countries) cannot be made to bear the burden of historical emissions in the name of ‘higher ambition’, as the 31st session of the UN climate conference (COP31) entered crunch time for negotiations to reach a consensus-based outcome in Antalya, Türkiye.Delivering the country’s national statement at the Conference, Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav said developing countries cannot be asked to choose between climate action and their legitimate right to development, decent living standards, health and education, adding that equitable access to the remaining carbon budget is non-negotiable.He also cautioned against unilateral trade measures (such as EU’s carbon border tax) that penalise developing countries under the guise of climate action, and called upon developed countries to honestly and expeditiously fulfil their climate finance obligations.Yadav’s remarks assume significance as developed countries, mainly EU nations, Switzerland and New Zealand, do not appear to be forthcoming in delivering on climate finance and even resisted progress on talks to clarify the tripling of adaptation finance. Even the latest COP31 draft text on climate finance indicates continued divisions among developed and developing nations.Similarly, trade measures such as the EU's carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) have not gone down well with countries like India and China. CBAM, which entered its operational regime on Jan 1, is a tool to put a price, through imposing a border tax, on carbon-intensive goods, like iron and steel, aluminium and cement, that are entering the 27 EU nations.India opposed the proposal from the time it was conceived, arguing that such a unilateral move placed an additional burden on businesses in developing economies due to embedded emissions in their products.Stressing that the success of COP31 must be assessed through tangible implementation, the delivery of resources to those who need them and the scaling up of proven solutions, Yadav called for dialogue to build trust, consensus to uphold equity and action to deliver climate justice.Emphasising the COP31 theme of ‘Dialogue, Consensus and Action’, he said that honest dialogue, equity-based consensus and urgent action must guide global climate efforts.

articles.title: 17 deaths, six days of pursuit: ‘Kabra’, the tusker, finally tranquilised in Surguja
articles.summary: Chhattisgarh’s rogue tusker ‘Kabra’, linked to 17 deaths, was tranquilised in Surguja after a six-day pursuit; officials plan radio-collaring and relocation.
articles.body: Raipur: For six months, villages across Chhattisgarh’s Surguja division lived in fear of an elephant known as ‘Kabra’. Linked to 17 deaths, the tusker had become a major challenge for forest officials, forcing residents to stay indoors after dark, schools to shut and roads to close as a precaution.On Wednesday, after six days of pursuit through the forests, a team of wildlife veterinarians and forest personnel finally tranquilised Kabra near the foothills of Ramgarh.Two trained kumki elephants, Duryodhan and Teerathram, played a crucial role in the operation. A veterinarian riding one of them got within darting range and successfully fired the tranquiliser.But tranquilising Kabra was only half the battle. Surrounded by a herd of around 17 elephants, the tusker had to be secured and separated from the others before being moved to safety.The operation had faced several setbacks. On Monday, the kumkis encountered Kabra, but the dart missed. Tracking him remained difficult as the herd moved through the forests of Sarma, Chakeri and Tendutikra under Udaipur forest range.By Tuesday night, the herd had reached Tendutikra forest. Villagers braved the bitter cold, keeping watch alongside forest personnel as the elephants moved dangerously close to settlements.The breakthrough came on Wednesday when the herd reached the lower slopes of Ramgarh hill. The veterinarian successfully darted Kabra, who collapsed under sedation. Forest personnel then began securing him and moving the other elephants away.Chief conservator of forests (wildlife), Surguja, Pranay Mishra, confirmed the operation. “Kabra has been tranquilised. Further procedures are underway,” he said.The department plans to fit the elephant with a radio collar and relocate him to a designated rescue centre for monitoring.Was Kabra in musth?Wildlife observer Nitin Singhvi has raised the possibility that Kabra was in musth, a temporary physiological condition in male elephants associated with elevated testosterone levels and, in some cases, heightened aggression.Elephant behaviour expert Ajay Desai has noted that some males in musth can become extremely aggressive and perceive approaching people or animals as threats. However, Kabra’s condition has not been confirmed through a veterinary assessment.Experts have urged villagers to maintain a safe distance from elephants and avoid provoking them by shouting, throwing stones or attempting to chase them away.Six months of fear in SurgujaLocal reports have linked Kabra to 17 deaths, although an official consolidated tally has not been released.The situation disrupted daily life across several villages. The Penderkhi-Chakeri road was temporarily closed, while nearly 20 schools in and around Sarma, Basen and Chakeri reportedly remained shut on Monday.Families avoided stepping outdoors after dark, with many staying awake through the night to watch for the herd.Kabra’s tranquilisation has brought some relief, but the operation is not over. articles.title: HC seeks restoration plan for Jagadish Bose’s dilapidated Giridih home
articles.summary: Jharkhand HC launches suo motu PIL on Jagadish Chandra Bose’s dilapidated Giridih home-museum, seeks restoration plan, affidavit, and opening of his iron chest.
articles.body: Ranchi: Jharkhand high court on Wednesday initiated a suo motu PIL over the deteriorating condition of Shanti Bhavan, the residence-cum-museum of eminent scientist Jagadish Chandra Bose in Giridih.Bose, a pioneer in radio science and plant physiology, lived at Shanti Bhavan. It ordered that the chest be opened under supervision and its contents made accessible.
